### Add datum leaders

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-10-18 (Revit 2020).

**What it does:** add the elbow to these grid and level heads in this view.

Adds the elbow - Add Elbow - to the heads of grids and levels in one view, at every end showing a bubble or at the start or end only, for many datums at once.

**How to use it**

1. Open the model in Revit and connect Heron: press **Heron** on the Heron tab, so its heron turns orange.
2. Select what it works on in Revit (elements) - or name it in the same request, and Heron finds it first.
3. Turn **Changes** on in Heron's **Settings** (Heron tab).
4. In a Claude chat, ask in your own words, for example *"add elbows to the grid heads in this view"*. Say the values under **You say** in the same sentence.

<a id="create-grids"></a>

### Create grids

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-11-26 (Revit 2020).

**What it does:** set out a whole grid from bay spacings.

Sets out a whole column grid from a start point and a list of bay dimensions - both directions, named the way a drawing names them, in one pass. The setting-out job as it is actually described: *"6000, 6000, 7500, 6000 across; 8000, 8000 up"*. **TWO INPUTS, ONE TOOL.** Two explicit points are right when the line is already known. For a bay layout they mean working out every coordinate by hand first, and for twelve grids in two directions that is where the mistakes come from - so the bay dimensions are the other input, which is how a drawing states one. **THEY ARE GAPS, NOT POSITIONS**, and both readings look sensible. Four of them make FIVE grids: the first sits at the start point and each gap steps to the next. Read as positions they give one grid too few and every line in the wrong place. **THE NAME HAS TO INCREMENT THE WAY A DRAWING DOES.** Letters run A to Z then AA, AB - not A to Z and stop, and not A1. Numbers run from whatever the start is. **VERSION 2 DRAWS GRIDS BETWEEN POINTS GIVEN AS WELL** - `gridLines`, named by `gridNames` - each line level, its ends forced onto one height, one whose ends differ in height refused. A grid Revit will not make undoes the whole call. **VERSION 5: A NAME ALREADY TAKEN IS SKIPPED, AND THE REST ARE MADE** - the owner's one rule for levels, grids and project reference planes (D-207). A grid whose name a grid in the project already has, or an earlier grid in the same call, ignoring capitals, is not made; `skipped` names each one and the grid holding the name, `findings` says how many were skipped beside how many were made, and only when every grid asked for is skipped is nothing made and `refused` says so. Versions 2 to 4 refused the whole call on one clash. **VERSION 3 ALSO SETS OUT A RADIAL GRID** - arcs about one centre over a sweep, and spokes out from it - named by Revit and read back. **The bay dimensions are MILLIMETRES, divided by 304.8 (D-71).** The start point is internal FEET, converted from millimetres by the add-in (D-67). ASSUMES AN OPEN TRANSACTION and does not open one (Golden Rule 16).

<a id="create-levels"></a>

### Create levels

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-11-26 (Revit 2020).

**What it does:** add storeys to the project.

Creates levels at the elevations given - one level or many - and reports what each one ended up at and what it ended up called. **A NAME ALREADY TAKEN IS SKIPPED, AND THE REST ARE MADE** (version 3, the owner's one rule for levels, grids and project reference planes, D-207). A level whose name a level in the project already has, or an earlier level in the same call, is not made; `skipped` names each one, its height and the level that holds the name, and every other level asked for is made. Only when every level asked for is skipped is nothing made, and `refused` says so. **A NAME ALREADY TAKEN WAS REFUSED BEFORE ANY LEVEL WAS CREATED** (version 2, when CREATE_LEVEL was merged in). Every name asked for is checked against the project's levels and against the other names in the call, ignoring capitals as Revit does, and one clash creates nothing: `refused` says which name clashed with which level. Version 1 created the level first and named it second, so a clash left a real level in the model under whatever Revit called it - `Level 7` when `Level 3` was asked for. `namedAs` still returns the name each level actually has, and `nameRefused` the ones whose name did not take. **A LEVEL REVIT WILL NOT CREATE IS NAMED, NEVER DROPPED** (version 2). Each refusal is recorded against its height and the whole job is then undone - nothing kept, one request one change (Article 8). Version 1 let it vanish and returned one level fewer with nothing said. It makes the levels and nothing else - `noViewsMade`, and the note below the contract. **THE ELEVATION IS READ BACK AS `ProjectElevation`.** That is the one in the same space as everything else in the model. `Elevation` is measured from whatever the level type's base says, so reading it back would confirm a number that was never in question and miss a survey offset entirely. `REPORT_LEVEL_ELEVATIONS` is the fragment that says whether the two differ on this model. **AN ELEVATION THAT ALREADY HAS A LEVEL IS SKIPPED, NOT STACKED.** Two levels at the same height is legal in Revit and is almost never wanted - it makes every view range and every "which level is this on" answer ambiguous, and it is the shape a re-run of this job takes if nothing guards it. **IT DOES NOT SPACE THEM.** *"Four more floors at 3.5 m"* is arithmetic, and arithmetic between two Revit calls belongs to the host (D-01). Handing this fragment a count and a spacing would put a second idea of what a storey height is inside the library.

<a id="list-grids"></a>

### List grids

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-10-18 (Revit 2020).

**What it does:** every column grid line in the project, in the order a drawing reads them.

Collects the project's column grids and reports each one's name and which way it runs - and, when asked, where each two cross, in millimetres (version 3) - and the spacing from each grid to the next one running the same way, square to them, in millimetres (version 4). **Grid names are not sortable as text, and this is the case that proves it.** A normal grid runs 1 to 12 one way and A to N the other. Sorted as strings, "10" comes before "2" - so the list reads 1, 10, 11, 12, 2, 3, and a modeller scanning for grid 3 finds it in the wrong half. The numbers are compared as numbers and the letters as letters, which is how the drawing reads. **Which way each grid runs is on the row**, because that is what somebody actually wants: *"which grid is nearest"* and *"is this on grid 5"* both depend on knowing whether 5 is a north-south line or an east-west one, and no name says. **LINKED MODELS ARE READ ONLY WHEN ASKED FOR (version 2, D-59).** With `includeLinks` absent this answers for this model alone, exactly as the proof measured. With it set, every loaded link is read too and `linksSearched` says how many were: set and 0 means "you asked, and none are loaded", which is a different answer from host-only. Each link's grids are listed in `linkedMatches`, in the same order, with their direction turned into this model's terms when the link is placed rotated. **NOTHING FROM A LINK IS EVER SELECTED OR CARRIED** - `elements` and `notLinear` stay this model's own; the chain revives ids against this model, and a linked id that happens to be in use here binds an unrelated element (FRAGMENT-ISSUES row 75). Links nested inside a link are not read, and are counted in the answer. This is version 2; version 1's proof no longer describes the code, and the fragment is DRAFT until it is proved again.

<a id="maximize-datum-extents"></a>

### Maximize datum extents

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-09-09 (Revit 2024).

**What it does:** the grids only go half way, make them all reach the same line.

Stretches grids and levels to span the whole model, so every grid of the same direction ends on exactly the same line. The *"some grids are short and they all stop in a different place"* tidy-up, done to the datum's own 3D extent so every view set to model extent picks it up. **DO NOT WORK THE LENGTH OUT AND PUSH A LONGER CURVE IN.** Two separate things go wrong with that, and the first is silent. Setting a grid's curve in a view is refused - *"the curve is unbound or not coincident with the original"* - and it is refused even when the grid is handed back its OWN curve, unchanged. So that error is not telling you the geometry is off, and checking the maths harder is wasted time. Revit's own maximize call is the one that works. **AND A MODEL BOUNDING BOX IS A POISONED NUMBER.** Every sheet carries a nominal box in model space about a hundred feet across, and cameras sit outside the building, so a whole-model box comes back far larger than the building. Grids extended to it are half as long again as anything real. Nothing here measures the model: the maximize call decides the extent. **THE RESULT IS NEVER SHORTER THAN WHAT YOU STARTED WITH.** Revit's idea of the model for this purpose includes the datums themselves, so the answer is the union of the building and the existing grids - which is why a grid that already reached further out keeps its length and pulls the others to it. **A VIEW WHERE AN END WAS DRAGGED SHORT WILL NOT SHOW THE CHANGE.** That end is on a view-specific extent, which overrides the shared one, and the fix then looks as if it did nothing in exactly the view somebody is looking at. Those are found and named rather than left to be discovered. There is no margin: the call lands flush on the extent, so a grid can finish exactly level with the slab edge with no overhang. Drafting overhang is a separate move, and the curve-setting route above is not available to make it. ASSUMES AN OPEN TRANSACTION and does not open one (Golden Rule 16).

<a id="propose-levels-from-point-cloud"></a>

### Propose levels from point cloud

**DRAFT - runs in a chat, and its answer says so.** It changes nothing in the model, so it is not refused, but it has not been proved on a real model yet.

**What it does:** which heights a linked point cloud shows a floor, a roof or the ground at, proposed as candidate levels.

Reads a sample of a linked point cloud's points, sorts their heights into thin horizontal bands, and reports each band holding far more points than the bands around it as a CANDIDATE level - its height in millimetres and in the project's own units, what share of the points it holds, how strongly it stands out from its neighbours (HIGH, MEDIUM or LOW), and the nearest level already in the model with the distance to it. It also reports how many points were read and the lowest and highest height among them. It creates nothing. **A CANDIDATE IS NOT A LEVEL (D-33).** A dense horizontal layer of points is a horizontal surface - a floor slab, a ceiling, a roof, a canopy, the ground. Which of them is a level is the modeller's call, and every answer says so in words. The heights are handed on as `candidateElevationsMm` so that, once the modeller has said yes to some of them, CREATE_LEVELS can make those - never on this card's own word. **A SCAN TAKEN FROM OUTSIDE HAS NO FLOORS IN IT.** A street scan sees the ground and the facades, and at best a canopy, an eave or a parapet. A facade spreads its points evenly up its whole height, so it makes no candidate; the ground and the roof line do. Every answer says that an outside-only scan gives ground and roof or eaves only, so "two candidates" is never read as "a two-storey building". **IT ANSWERS "NO POINT CLOUD", NEVER A GUESS.** A model with no point cloud linked is refused with that said, and so is a name that matches none or more than one. A box that holds no points answers with no candidates and says why, rather than an empty list that reads as "nothing horizontal here". **WHERE THE HEIGHTS ARE MEASURED FROM.** From the internal origin, the same space as each level's Project Elevation and as the millimetres CREATE_LEVELS takes. The box is passed to Revit in model coordinates, as RevitAPI.xml says the filter must be; the points read are carried through the cloud's own transform. Points that land more than a metre outside the cloud's extent in Revit are said, with a CHECK line, because that is the shape of points read in the scan's own coordinates instead.

<a id="report-level-elevations"></a>

### Report level elevations

**DRAFT - runs in a chat, and its answer says so.** It changes nothing in the model, so it is not refused, but it has not been proved on a real model yet.

**What it does:** whether this model's level heights can be trusted in a calculation.

Reports every level's TWO heights side by side and says, in one word, whether they disagree on this model. **A LEVEL HAS TWO HEIGHTS AND ONLY ONE OF THEM IS IN THE SAME SPACE AS THE MODEL'S GEOMETRY.** `Elevation` is measured from whatever the level type's "Elevation Base" says - Project or Shared. `ProjectElevation` is always measured from the project origin. Every XYZ the API hands back - a location point, a bounding box, a solid's vertices, a ray's origin - is in project-internal coordinates. So the moment a level height meets a coordinate, `ProjectElevation` is the only one that belongs there. **WHY IT IS A FRAGMENT AND NOT A NOTE IN A DOCUMENT.** On a test model the two numbers are identical and nothing shows. On a real site model with a survey offset, every height answer is wrong by exactly that offset - silently, with a plausible number. That is this project's defining failure shape, and a document warning about it cannot tell you whether TODAY'S model is affected. This can, and it prints the offset, which is exactly how wrong the answers would be. **THE VERDICT IS MEASURED, NEVER INFERRED FROM THE SETTING.** The "Elevation Base" parameter is reported because a person will want to see it, but nothing here branches on it: the API publishes no enum for its values, so "0 means Project" is an assumption, and its display text is localised. The verdict comes from subtracting the two elevations, which is true in any language. **A DIFFERENCE OF ZERO DOES NOT PROVE THE BASE IS PROJECT.** It also happens when the base is Shared and the shared origin simply sits on the project origin - true until somebody relocates the model. So a third verdict exists between the two obvious ones: NOT AFFECTED TODAY, BUT AT RISK, reported whenever the survey point carries a vertical offset that a single setting change would start applying. **CHECKING ONE LEVEL PROVES NOTHING ABOUT THE REST.** "Elevation Base" lives on the level TYPE, and two level types in one model may disagree - half on Project and half on Shared is legal. `typesDisagree` is reported for that case, because it is the version of this that survives a spot check. **LINKED MODELS ARE READ ONLY WHEN ASKED FOR (version 2, D-59).** With `includeLinks` absent this answers for this model alone, exactly as the proof measured. With it set, every loaded link's levels are carried through its first placement into this model's space and set against this model's level of the same NAME - *"is the architect's Level 2 at the same height as mine"* - and `linkedMatches` gives each link's count, then one line per linked level: its height here, this model's, and the difference in millimetres, or that no level here has that name. A file placed more than once at different heights is said, not averaged. `linksSearched` says how many links were read: set and 0 means "you asked, and none are loaded". **NOTHING FROM A LINK IS CARRIED** - `levels` and both dictionaries stay this model's own; they are keyed by ids the next step would look up here (FRAGMENT-ISSUES row 75). Links nested inside a link are not read, and are counted in the answer. This is version 2; version 1's proof no longer describes the code, and the fragment is DRAFT until it is proved again. **WHICH LEVELS ARE BUILDING STORIES, AND WHAT STANDS ON THE ONES THAT ARE NOT (version 3).** Every reply now carries `storeys`: each level's "Building Story" setting, and for every level NOT marked, how many model elements have that level as their level. An IFC export makes a storey only from a level marked Building Story, so elements on an unmarked level are put in another storey on the way out. An element's level is found in four steps and in this order, ending on an MEP curve's start level, because a duct keeps its level nowhere else. Only model elements are counted; views, sheets and annotation carry a level too and go into no storey. **Numbers, never a verdict** - an unmarked level with nothing on it is harmless, and one with elements on it is the modeller's call. When every level is marked the reply says so and names the levels it read, rather than printing a bare zero. Linked models are not read for this, whatever `includeLinks` says. Versions 1 and 2 above are kept as the record; this is version 3, and the fragment is DRAFT until it is proved again. **VERSION 7 - THE ONE DATUM TOOL: LEVELS AND GRIDS, HERE, IN A LINK, AND COPY-MONITORED.** CHECK_DATUMS_AGAINST_LINK is merged in. With `includeLinks` or a link named in `linkName`, this model's grids and levels are checked against the link's - matched by name, then by lining up, and each said aligned within the tolerance, off by how many millimetres and degrees, not checked and why, or only in one model - one row each in `report`, the datums off counted in `failures` and handed on in `failingIds` to select, `compared` the pairs measured. `toleranceMm`, `angleToleranceDeg` and `datums` (grids, levels or both) are the check's. Every grid or level here that copy-monitors a link is listed in `monitored`, with the link placement it watches, and is measured against that placement when links are asked for. A linked file placed more than once is never measured until the copy is named in `linkName` - every placement is named and the modeller asked, never the first one taken (D-207); a placement a datum here copy-monitors is named by that monitoring. Nothing is changed. DRAFT until version 7 is proved. **IT IS ALSO THE LIST OF LEVELS** (version 4, when LIST_LEVELS was merged in): the levels bottom to top, handed on as `elements`, each one's height in millimetres as its level head shows it in `elevationsMm` and from the project origin in `projectElevationsMm`, one line per level in `findings` with the two said apart where they differ, and each linked level's own level head beside its height here. DRAFT until version 4 is proved.

<a id="set-datum-bubbles"></a>

### Set datum bubbles

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-09-09 (Revit 2024).

**What it does:** the grid bubbles are on the wrong side in this view.

Shows, hides or flips the bubble - the head carrying the grid or level name - on grids and levels, in one view. The sheet job: bubbles on the wrong side of a plan, or missing from the end somebody reads from. **Bubbles are per END and per VIEW, and this changes one view.** That is correct for bubbles and it is NOT how datum extents behave, where the model type is shared across views. Confusing the two is how somebody "fixes" one plan and finds they have changed twenty. **Flip is not one call.** Revit offers only show, hide and ask, per end - so a flip is read both ends, then hide one and show the other. Two cases have no obvious flip and are decided explicitly rather than silently doing nothing: with NEITHER end visible one is shown, because something has to appear or the flip looks broken; with BOTH visible one is hidden, which is what flipped should mean. **End 0 and End 1 are the datum's own two ends, not left and right.** Which looks left depends on the direction the grid was drawn and on the view. If a batch flips half of them the way you wanted and half the other way, the grids were drawn in opposite directions - that is the model, not this fragment, and the fix is to name the end rather than to flip. **Bubbles mean nothing in a 3D view.** Those are skipped and counted rather than passed over silently. ASSUMES AN OPEN TRANSACTION and does not open one (Golden Rule 16).

| | |
|---|---|
| **Kind** | Changes the model (`MODIFY`) |
| **Reached by** | asking in a Claude chat |
| **Works on** | what is selected in Revit: elements |
| **You say** | **view** - a view, by name - resolved BY NAME in Revit; a name matching twice is refused<br>**mode** - text |
| **You get** | changed, findings |
| **Built for Revit** | 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024, 2025, 2026, 2027 |
| **Proved on Revit** | 2024 |
| **Capability** | `SET_DATUM_BUBBLES` |

**How to use it**

1. Open the model in Revit and connect Heron: press **Heron** on the Heron tab, so its heron turns orange.
2. Select what it works on in Revit (elements) - or name it in the same request, and Heron finds it first.
3. Turn **Changes** on in Heron's **Settings** (Heron tab).
4. In a Claude chat, ask in your own words, for example *"the grid bubbles are on the wrong side"*. Say the values under **You say** in the same sentence.
5. Heron makes the change as **one entry in Revit's Undo list**. With **Ask to Keep** on, Revit asks **Keep or Discard** first; Ctrl+Z takes it back.

Other ways to ask: *"flip the bubbles"* · *"turn the level heads on"*

<a id="set-datum-extent-type"></a>

### Set datum extent type

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-11-02 (Revit 2020).

**What it does:** make this grid 2d in this view, or put it back to 3d, and say which it was.

Reads whether each grid or level end is on its shared 3D extent or on a view-specific 2D one, and sets it either way. **ONLY ONE DIRECTION EXISTED.** `RESET_DATUM_EXTENTS` writes `DatumExtentType.Model`, which is 2D to 3D - it throws away the per-view override somebody made by dragging an end. Measured 2026-09-18, `SetDatumExtentType` appears exactly ONCE in the whole library, at `reset-datum-extents/impl/any/fragment.cs:60`, and the value is always `Model`. So a modeller could be handed back the shared extent and could never be given a view-specific one - which is the ordinary drafting job of shortening one grid in one view without touching the other twenty. **AND THE STATE COULD NOT BE ASKED FOR.** `MAXIMIZE_DATUM_EXTENTS` calls `GetDatumExtentTypeInView` and reports which ends are view-specific, but only as accounting while it stretches things. Nothing answered *"is this grid 2D or 3D in this view"* without modifying the model to find out. So this reads first and reports what it found BEFORE changing it, the way `SET_VIEW_PROPERTIES` and `SET_VIEW_PROPERTIES` both read and set. **EXTENTS ARE SHARED AND BUBBLES ARE NOT, AND CONFUSING THEM CHANGES TWENTY VIEWS.** `SET_DATUM_BUBBLES` states it plainly: bubbles are per end and per view; the MODEL extent is shared across every view. Setting an end back to `Model` here therefore reaches every view that shows it, not just this one. That is the point of the call and it is said out loud rather than discovered. **BOTH ENDS ARE HANDLED SEPARATELY**, because only one is usually dragged. Version 2 takes many views at once - `views` - and names every datum an end of which Revit would not change, in `refused`. ASSUMES AN OPEN TRANSACTION and does not open one (Golden Rule 16).

| | |
|---|---|
| **Kind** | Changes the model (`MODIFY`) |
| **Reached by** | asking in a Claude chat |
| **Works on** | what is selected in Revit: elements |
| **You say** | **view** - a view, by name - resolved BY NAME in Revit; a name matching twice is refused; optional<br>**views** - comma separated, resolved BY NAME in Revit; a name matching twice is refused; optional<br>**view specific** - yes or no - true or false |
| **You get** | changed, findings, ends changed |
| **Built for Revit** | 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024, 2025, 2026, 2027 |
| **Proved on Revit** | 2020 |
| **Capability** | `SET_DATUM_EXTENT_TYPE` |

**How to use it**

1. Open the model in Revit and connect Heron: press **Heron** on the Heron tab, so its heron turns orange.
2. Select what it works on in Revit (elements) - or name it in the same request, and Heron finds it first.
3. Turn **Changes** on in Heron's **Settings** (Heron tab).
4. In a Claude chat, ask in your own words, for example *"make this grid 2d in this view"*. Say the values under **You say** in the same sentence.
5. Heron makes the change as **one entry in Revit's Undo list**. With **Ask to Keep** on, Revit asks **Keep or Discard** first; Ctrl+Z takes it back.

Other ways to ask: *"change the grid from 3d to 2d"* · *"set this level back to 3d"*
